director.chapterArc: A night of helplessness drives Jab from futile magical intervention into a near-fatal lapse; the choking crisis forces him back to practical care. Self-reproach then becomes method: he discovers that desire corrupts the Kindling’s answer, establishes emotional neutrality as a rule, and successfully anticipates the next fever wave. Dawn brings depleted forward motion, brief familial humor, and a final reversal at the flooded creek, where Tonk’s quiet refusal exposes remembered terror beneath Jab’s controlled reassurance.
director.restraintNote: Keep Original Calder grounded and unhurried. The choking sequence gains pressure through delayed bodily response and clear mechanics, not speed. Treat the Kindling discovery as a quiet operational insight, never mystical spectacle. Grief surfaces only in Jab’s inventory of failure and the memory of his parents; the flood ending stays cold, spatially precise, and protective rather than openly panicked.

cues.delivery: Let the repeated sound and useless inventory reveal that Jab has reached the edge of his resources; remain clinically calm, with dread held beneath practical observation.
cues.from: It ran its forty minutes and then it kept going, and the bark had been in him since dusk and was doing nothing that Jab could see, and at some point past the middle of the night Tonk stopped saying words and only made a sound on the out-breath, over and over, low, the same note.
cues.through: And he had a piece of river metal at his throat that could cut through anything in the fir stand and could not touch what was in his brother's leg.
cues.reason: The bad hour ceases to be routine and becomes an admission of helplessness.

cues.delivery: Give the bucket image one dry flicker of self-recognition; the humor is exhausted and corrective, never a release from danger.
cues.from: He changed things. He tried both hands. He tried a hand on the chest and a hand on the leg, above the wrapping, where the heat was worst and where the skin was so tight it felt like something about to split. He tried breathing out while he pushed, the way his father's aunt had made him breathe out on the gravel bar. He tried saying it, which he was glad nobody heard. He tried holding the metal in his other fist so that it would be in the circuit, which felt clever for about four seconds and then felt like a boy shaking a bucket to make it rain.
cues.through: He changed things. He tried both hands. He tried a hand on the chest and a hand on the leg, above the wrapping, where the heat was worst and where the skin was so tight it felt like something about to split. He tried breathing out while he pushed, the way his father's aunt had made him breathe out on the gravel bar. He tried saying it, which he was glad nobody heard. He tried holding the metal in his other fist so that it would be in the circuit, which felt clever for about four seconds and then felt like a boy shaking a bucket to make it rain.
cues.reason: Jab briefly sees the absurdity of his desperate improvisation.

cues.delivery: Narrow the focus to airway, distance, and the three lost heartbeats. Preserve every physical step; pressure comes from Jab’s abnormal slowness, not a rushed read.
cues.from: Then Tonk coughed and the cough went wrong.
cues.through: He had never in his life had that happen. He had always simply been where he needed to be, fast, without the between part; his body had done that for him since he was nine years old on a slick bar with fish coming in. This time he came up off his knees and the world went sideways and gray, and he had to put a hand down on the ground and wait for it, three whole beats, listening to his brother not breathe.
cues.reason: The magical failure becomes an immediate threat to Tonk’s life.

cues.delivery: Firm, close, and functional—the cadence of a caretaker lending Tonk his calm while checking that each breath returns.
cues.from: "I've got you. I've got you. Cough it out. Good. Again."
cues.through: "I've got you. I've got you. Cough it out. Good. Again."
cues.reason: Jab stabilizes Tonk through direct, protective instruction.

cues.delivery: Thin and homesick, with no theatrical pleading; let the impossible wish arrive on dwindling breath.
cues.reason: Tonk’s request is intimate, weakened, and beyond Jab’s power to grant.

cues.delivery: Make the self-indictment plain and unsentimental. The spoken rule is a binding protocol made from guilt, not an emotional confession.
cues.from: Best part of an hour, he thought. He had spent the best part of an hour of the worst night they had had, pushing at a door, while the fire went down and his brother lay flat.
cues.through: He meant it about as much as a man means anything at that hour. But he made himself say the whole of it out loud, to fix it: "You don't get to try things on him. You try them on you, or you don't try them."
cues.reason: Jab converts the cost of his mistake into a prohibition he can obey.

cues.delivery: Hold the question inward, then let the history of ordinary usefulness accumulate toward the parents without swelling. Land the final inability with exhausted factual weight.
cues.from: He sat back on his heels in the dark, and put his hand flat on his own breastbone, over the metal, over the small stubborn warmth that had been there for four years and had never once done anything he had not asked it to.
cues.through: It did not tell him. It sat there being warm, the way it had while he split fish and cut willow and hauled logs and lit a blade over a log jam, the way it had been while his parents went down the river in the dark and he lay on a gravel slope with his brother's blood on his hands and could not do one single thing about any of it.
cues.reason: The new power is measured against the one catastrophe it could not prevent.

cues.delivery: Use dry family warmth and precise timing. Jab tells it to keep Tonk moving; the remembered laughter should briefly humanize the road without erasing fatigue.
cues.through: "Not that day," Jab said. "He laughed about it for eleven years after."
cues.reason: A small comic memory provides controlled relief before the terrain turns dangerous.

cues.delivery: Read the flood as a physical calculation: width, grinding stones, moving trees, speed. Keep awe out of it; Jab is measuring a lethal obstacle.
cues.from: It was forty feet across and the color of tea with milk in it, and it was not making the noise that water makes going over stones — it was making the low grinding noise water makes when it is rolling stones along the bottom. Whole trees were going down it. As Jab stood there with the frame on his hips and the cold coming up off the water into his face, a root ball the size of a house came around the upstream bend, turned over once, and went past them at the speed of a man running.
cues.through: Somewhere under all of that there was a crossing. The Elder had drawn it on the table: a wide shallow braid where the creek spread out over gravel, knee-deep in the ordinary autumn, a thing a loaded man walked across without taking off his boots.
cues.reason: The destroyed crossing converts landscape into immediate survival threat.

cues.delivery: Small, close to Jab’s ear, and stripped of childish animation; the repetition begins as recognition of remembered danger.
cues.from: "Jab," said Tonk, behind his ear. He had gone very quiet in the last hundred steps. "Jab. That's water."
cues.through: "Jab," said Tonk, behind his ear. He had gone very quiet in the last hundred steps. "Jab. That's water."
cues.reason: Tonk’s quietness signals trauma rather than ordinary alarm.

cues.delivery: Give Jab an intentionally ordinary, almost conversational steadiness. Beneath it, he is constructing safety one promise at a time and must not sound certain beyond what he can guarantee.
cues.from: "I know it is. We're not going in it." Jab took his eyes off the flood and made himself say the next part in the voice he used about jays. "We're going to stand here a minute and I'm going to look at it, and then we're going to go along the bank and find a better place, and you're going to help me look. All right?"
cues.through: "I know it is. We're not going in it." Jab took his eyes off the flood and made himself say the next part in the voice he used about jays. "We're going to stand here a minute and I'm going to look at it, and then we're going to go along the bank and find a better place, and you're going to help me look. All right?"
cues.reason: Jab masks his own assessment to prevent Tonk’s fear from escalating.

cues.delivery: Quiet, literal, and withdrawn—not petulant. Let the refusal show that reassurance has not reached the place where Tonk is afraid.
cues.from: "I don't want to help," he said.
cues.through: "I don't want to help," he said.
cues.reason: The chapter closes on the child’s subdued inability to participate in Jab’s coping ritual.
